report.source_text: Background ocular history includes bilateral keratoconus, with a previous 3 right penetrating keratoplasties, with moderate keratoconus remaining in the left eye, predominantly managed with a rigid gas permeable lens. Unaided visual acuity of the right eye was counting fingers improving to 6/15 with pinhole, left eye aided visual acuity was 6/7.5 with a rigid contact lens in-situ. Intraocular pressures were RE 10 mmHg and LE 6 mmHg. Eye movements were full and unrestricted in both eyes. Color plate testing with Ishihara was full and brisk in each eye. Monocular confrontational visual field testing was clear of obvious abnormality in either eye. Pupils were equal and reactive to light with no sign of relative afferent pupillary defect. Exophthalmometry was R 15 mm—112 mm—L 16 mm. Slit lamp examination showed an intact right globe. The right corneal graft was reasonably clear with no sign of rejection or dehiscence, whilst the left cornea showed signs of moderate keratoconus. Both anterior chambers were deep and quiet. The crystalline lens was clear in both eyes, and the vitreous was quiet. Dilated fundus examination showed no abnormality to the left eye, however a raised white retinal lesion was noted in the right eye, superior-temporal to the optic disc approximately 4-disc diameters away and approximately 1.5-disc diameters in length

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 41-year-old male with history of bilateral keratoconus and three prior right penetrating keratoplasties presented after high-energy trauma (car vs bicycle collision) with multiorgan injuries and right tripod facial fracture. Initial CT imaging revealed a hyperdense right intraocular lesion raising concern for retained intraocular foreign body (IOFB), prompting ophthalmology consultation. Comprehensive ophthalmic examination demonstrated an intact right globe without signs of penetrating injury, with visual acuity counting fingers improving to 6/15 with pinhole, normal intraocular pressure (10 mmHg), full eye movements, and no relative afferent pupillary defect. Dilated fundus examination identified a raised white retinal lesion located superotemporal to the optic disc (approximately 4-disc diameters away), confirmed on Optos widefield imaging. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) through the lesion demonstrated the pathognomonic 'double rocky and rolling' elevation pattern with no subretinal fluid, characteristic of scleral choroidal calcification. The superotemporal location corresponds anatomically to the superior oblique tendon insertion site. These findings confirmed the lesion represented benign scleral choroidal calcification rather than traumatic metallic foreign body, with no globe injury sustained from the trauma.
